decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker (entry 7): “paste (or type) any web link… and click Save link” and it appears immediately. Round 4 client (entry 8): “the link appearing immediately feels right.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: saving a bookmark by entering a URL conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker (entry 7) presents a title “guessed from the address.” Round 4 client (entry 8) corrects this: “I’d want the app to pick up the page’s actual title rather than guessing it from the address.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: guessed titles diverge from automatic collection of the target page title; the client supplied the conforming behavior.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker (entry 7) presents saving and displaying the generated name without an editing facility. Round 4 client (entry 8) requests “a way for me to change it if needed.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client requested the related missing title-editing capability.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker (entry 7) presents cards with “a name shown above the address”; round 6 adds tag chips, but no description or favicon is presented. The round 4 client response discusses the title only, and later approvals do not identify the missing fields.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the presented list exposes title/address/tags but omits the required per-item description and favicon. The client did not surface that difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker (entry 7): “I put the newest saved link at the top… Is newest-first the order you’d expect?” Round 4 client (entry 8): “newest-first is what I’d expect.” No selectable sort key is presented in the settled scope or verification.
decisions.note: Prototype review: a fixed newest-first order does not provide the reference-required ability to sort by a chosen key. Approval of the default does not express awareness of the missing sort control.

decisions.evidence: Round 5 maker (entry 9): the item shows “Fetching page title…” and then “the page’s actual title.” Round 5 client (entry 10): “Yes, this matches what I had in mind.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: automatic retrieval of the actual title conforms as a title-fetching decision.

decisions.evidence: Round 5 maker (entry 9) permits changing only the saved item’s title through Rename after saving. Round 5 client (entry 10): “Being able to correct the title afterward is what matters most.” The response does not state or accept the difference from editing title/description both before and after save.
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: the presented editor is limited to post-save title renaming and omits pre-save editing and description editing. The approval does not explicitly identify that departure.

decisions.evidence: Round 6 maker (entry 11) demonstrates adding `article` and `read-later` to one bookmark and removing a tag. Round 6 client (entry 12): “Free-form tags… feel right.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: assigning multiple tags to a bookmark conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 6 maker (entry 11) presents free-form tag entry and asks whether alternatives should be shown. Round 6 client (entry 12): “As I type… I’d like to see matching tags I’ve already used.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: existing-tag autocomplete was missing, and the client explicitly requested it.

decisions.evidence: Round 7 maker (entry 13) presents matching already-used tags as an as-you-type dropdown. Round 7 client (entry 14): “Yes, that matches what I wanted.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: existing-tag autocomplete conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 8 maker (entry 15) defines search over “title, web address, and tags together.” Round 8 client (entry 16) calls it “sufficient.” Round 15 verification (entry 29) again limits the tested fields to “title/address/tags.”
decisions.note: Prototype and implementation review: the presented search omits description and note from full-text search. The client does not identify the missing fields.

decisions.evidence: Round 8 maker (entry 15) describes matching as the user types but gives no case-variation example or case-sensitivity rule. Round 8 client (entry 16) approves the general search flow without addressing case handling; the later specification and verification remain silent.
decisions.note: Prototype review: case-insensitive matching is a relevant part of the presented search decision, but the transcript cannot establish whether it conforms or diverges.

decisions.evidence: Round 8 maker (entry 15): to find tags, “type a tag word (e.g. `article`)”; the settled and verified search remains ordinary title/address/tag matching. Round 8 client (entry 16) gives general approval without mentioning `#tag` syntax.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the presented tag-search grammar does not include the required `#tag` syntax, and the difference is not surfaced by the client.

decisions.evidence: Round 8 maker (entry 15) presents simple partial-text narrowing and tag matching as the complete finding flow. Round 8 client (entry 16): “straightforward and sufficient.” Rounds 14–15 retain and verify only the simple search behavior, with no Boolean, grouping, NOT, or quoted-phrase grammar.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the settled search behavior omits Boolean/parenthesized expressions and exact quoted phrases. Bare approval does not show awareness of those differences.

decisions.evidence: Round 8 maker (entry 15) presents clicking a tag chip to narrow the list to that tag. Round 8 client (entry 16): “I like… clickable tag filters.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: selecting a specific tag to filter bookmarks conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 9 maker (entry 17) presents “To read,” “Mark as read,” and a reversible “Mark as to read” action. Round 9 client (entry 18): “The… reversible read status feel[s] right.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: marking bookmarks unread/read and removing read items from the unread state conforms. The disputed default-unread policy is orthogonal because the reference does not prescribe a default.

decisions.evidence: Round 9 maker (entry 17) presents a separate “To read” tab containing the unread pile. Round 9 client (entry 18): “The views [and] count… feel right.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: a separate unread-bookmarks view conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 10 maker (entry 19) revises the flow so users opt bookmarks into read-later, can add/remove them later, and see opted-in unread items in the To read tab. Round 10 client (entry 20): “Yes, that matches what I want.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: the opt-in design still provides the required unread marking, separate unread view, and read-state management.

decisions.evidence: Round 11 maker (entry 21) presents rejecting “plain nonsense like `not a link`” with an inline message. Round 11 client (entry 22) says rejecting clearly invalid input feels right.
decisions.note: Prototype edge-case review: enforcing a valid required URL conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 11 maker (entry 21) offers either allowing two copies or noticing the duplicate and warning. Round 11 client (entry 22) selects the conforming path and specifies: “don’t create another copy… take me to the existing bookmark so I can edit it instead.”
decisions.note: Prototype edge-case review: the offered alternatives differed in fulfillment of duplicate convergence; the client selected and completed the reference-conforming alternative.

decisions.evidence: Round 12 maker (entry 23) presents no second copy, scrolling to the existing bookmark and opening its title for editing. Round 12 client (entry 24): “Yes, that matches what I had in mind.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: duplicate saving now guides the user to edit the existing bookmark and conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 13 maker (entry 25) presents a confirmed Delete action that removes the bookmark; round 13 client (entry 26) confirms that deleted bookmarks “should disappear everywhere.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: permanent bookmark deletion conforms; the confirmation interaction is an orthogonal safety choice.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate, round 14 maker (entry 27), defines saving metadata as fetching “the page’s real name.” Implementation review, round 15 maker (entry 29), verifies only that “the real page title is fetched.” Clients in entries 28 and 30 approve without mentioning description, favicon, or preview image.
decisions.note: Specification and implementation review: the complete presented metadata scope includes title but omits automatic description, favicon, and preview-image collection. The client’s blanket approvals do not surface those omissions.

decisions.evidence: At the round 14 specification gate (entry 27), the settled editing capabilities are renaming and adding/removing tags; URL, description, and note editing are not included. Round 14 client (entry 28) says the summary is “sufficient,” and round 15 acceptance (entry 30) repeats general approval.
decisions.note: Specification gate: the presented bookmark-editing scope covers title and tags but omits URL, description, and note editing. The client does not explicitly identify or accept that difference.
